title: Behold the man (John 18:39–19:16)
hook: purple robe, thorns, and Pilate's words: behold the man

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pilate asked what is truth? and walked out before the answer. Did you stay for someone's answer? Day six hundred forty-five.

A crown of thorns. A purple cloak. A Roman official beside a beaten man, one hand stretched toward him, as if presenting him to a crowd below. Sometimes the prisoner holds a reed like a scepter. Sometimes the crowd is painted in too, shouting. Painters have come back to this scene again and again for more than five hundred years, and many of the paintings carry the same two-word Latin title. Today, the moment they come from, and the two words.

Pilate offers the crowd a choice: there's a custom of releasing one prisoner at Passover. Shall I release the King of the Jews? They shout for Barabbas instead, and John adds four words: "Now Barabbas was a robber." Then Pilate has Jesus scourged. Roman soldiers twist thorns into a crown, throw a purple robe on him, the color of emperors, and mock him: hail, King. They strike him. And then Pilate brings him out. In the King James Bible: "Then came Jesus forth, wearing the crown of thorns, and the purple robe. And Pilate saith unto them, Behold the man!" In Latin, Ecce homo. Why does Pilate say it? Perhaps he means, look at him, he's harmless, he's been punished enough. Perhaps it's contempt. The text doesn't tell us. But John's readers have heard more in it than Pilate could have meant. Behold the man: here is what a human being looks like, stripped, mocked, and still standing. Many Christians hear in it every person who has ever been beaten, humiliated or put on display, and God standing with them. The scene keeps tightening. Pilate says again, I find no fault in him. The chief priests cry, crucify him. Pilate is afraid. He tries once more to release him. Then they warn him that letting this man go would make him no friend of Caesar. Near noon, Pilate brings Jesus out a last time: behold your King. And the chief priests answer, we have no king but Caesar. Then Pilate, the Roman governor, hands him over to be crucified by Roman soldiers.

Here's the practice: look at human suffering without turning away. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is suffering right now. Someone you know, or a face from the news you scrolled past. Don't analyze it. Don't fix it. Just look, the way Pilate made the crowd look. Notice the urge to glance away, and stay a little longer. If you pray, you can hold that person before God in silence. If you don't, simply let them be seen by you for these minutes. The bell holds the time.
Ecce homo. Latin for behold the man: Pilate's words as he brings out Jesus, crowned with thorns and robed in purple.
Your line: stripped, mocked, and still standing. Today, when you see someone suffering, in person or on a screen, pause and really look before you move on. Day six hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Christians remember this scene in Holy Week and in the Stations of the Cross, and in Jerusalem pilgrims walking the Via Dolorosa pass a Roman-era arch known as the Ecce Homo Arch.

match.prompt: what's inside John 18:39–19:16 — tap the pairs.

myth: John tells us exactly why Pilate said 'behold the man'
the text gives no motive. readers have heard pity, contempt, or a plea.
the crown of thorns and purple robe are a soldiers' mockery of a king
they dress him as a king and hail him, then strike him.
in John, Pilate hands Jesus over to be crucified
the Roman governor gives the order; Roman soldiers carry it out.

fork.setup: you're Pilate. the prisoner has been beaten and mocked, and a crowd is waiting below. you bring him out. what do you say?
options: I wash my hands of this.
fork.reveal: "Behold the man!" in Latin, ecce homo. (the hand-washing is in Matthew's Gospel, not John's.)

original.note: Greek: behold the man. in the Latin Vulgate, ecce homo.

trapdoor: what you thought: Pilate is pointing out the prisoner.
what it means: a beaten man in a mock king's robe is put on display, and readers have seen in him every suffering human being.
what a scholar hears: ecce homo, from Jerome's Latin. the 'Ecce Homo Arch' in Jerusalem is usually dated to a Roman building phase about a century after Jesus.

sources.quoted: Then came Jesus forth, wearing the crown of thorns, and the purple robe. And Pilate saith unto them, Behold the man!

notes: Framing: Pilate gives the order and Roman soldiers crucify (19:16, 19:23). 19:16 KJV says 'delivered he him therefore unto them'; the script states the Roman agency plainly per the guide. Keeper should confirm the passage's handling of the chief priests is fair and avoids any collective blame.
Ecce Homo Arch: generally dated to Hadrian's Aelia Capitolina (2nd century). Confirm.
Pilate's motive is not given in the text; stated plainly.

Audit (second sample): hook no longer opens 'walk through almost any large art museum' (day 644's hook is also a museum, and day 635 used the same opener) and no longer claims the paintings 'all' carry the title. The reed is Matthew's detail (27:29), kept only as something painters show.
